title: A Chinese Cancer Drug Just Beat the Global Gold Standard for Lung Cancer. It Is the First From Asia to Earn a Plenary at ASCO in 61 Years.
excerpt: Ivonescimab reduced the risk of death by 34 per cent in advanced squamous lung cancer. The results were published in The Lancet the same day. For Indian families watching air-pollution-driven cancer rates climb, the implications are significant.
body:
Lung cancer kills more people worldwide than any other malignancy. In India, it claims over 100,000 lives every year, a toll amplified by chronic exposure to air pollution in cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata. For the Indian diaspora, many of whom still have parents and extended family breathing that air, any advance in treatment carries personal weight.

On Sunday, at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting in Chicago, a Chinese biotech company presented data that no Asian pharmaceutical firm has ever been invited to share at this level. Akeso, headquartered in Guangdong, announced that its drug ivonescimab — a first-in-class bispecific antibody that simultaneously blocks PD-1 and VEGF — reduced the risk of death by 34 per cent in patients with advanced squamous non-small cell lung cancer, the most aggressive form of the disease.

The trial, called HARMONi-6, enrolled 532 patients in China and compared ivonescimab plus chemotherapy against tislelizumab (a PD-1 inhibitor) plus chemotherapy, the current standard of care. The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.66, meaning patients on ivonescimab were roughly a third less likely to die during the study period. The results were published simultaneously in The Lancet.

## Why This Matters Beyond China

This is the first time in ASCO's 61-year history that a cancer drug developed in China has been selected for the Plenary Session, the meeting's most prestigious scientific slot. It signals that Asia's pharmaceutical industry — long seen as a generics manufacturer — is now producing original therapeutics that compete with the best from the West.

For the Indian diaspora, the relevance runs in two directions. First, India and China share similar cancer epidemiology. Squamous non-small cell lung cancer accounts for roughly 30 per cent of all lung cancers in both countries, and its incidence is rising among non-smokers exposed to particulate matter. A treatment that works in a Chinese population is likely to show similar efficacy in South Asian patients.

Second, ivonescimab represents a new class of bispecific antibodies that could reshape how oncologists approach treatment. Unlike existing checkpoint inhibitors that target a single pathway, this drug hits two — the PD-1 immune checkpoint and the VEGF blood-supply pathway that tumours exploit to feed themselves. The dual mechanism may explain why it outperformed a drug that only blocks PD-1.

## The Numbers in Detail

The trial's primary endpoint was progression-free survival, which ivonescimab had already won in earlier data. The overall survival results announced today were a key secondary endpoint, and they held up across every subgroup the investigators tested. Patients with PD-L1-negative tumours — who typically respond poorly to immunotherapy — saw a comparable benefit. Those with brain or liver metastases also showed improvement.

The safety profile was described as manageable and consistent with prior clinical experience. The trial's sponsor, Summit Therapeutics, which holds rights to ivonescimab outside China, plans a conference call on Monday morning to discuss next steps, including regulatory submissions in the US.

## What This Means for NRI Families

India's National Cancer Registry estimates that lung cancer incidence in Indian men has risen 12 per cent in the last decade. For diaspora families with elderly parents in Indian metros, this trajectory is deeply personal. Access to ivonescimab will depend on how quickly it navigates US and Indian regulatory pathways, but the science is now in The Lancet, and the data are hard to argue with.

Meanwhile, Summit Therapeutics trades on Nasdaq under the ticker SMMT. For NRI investors who track biotech, the stock is worth watching — a successful US filing could transform the company's valuation. But the more consequential development is what this drug represents: a shift in where the world's best cancer science is coming from, and a new treatment option for a disease that hits close to home.
author: Diaspora Desk
